facts.statement: The genus Palaeochenoides was described by Shufeldt in 1916.
Fossils of Palaeochenoides date to the Late Oligocene.
Only one species, Palaeochenoides mioceanus, is currently known from this genus.
facts.quote: Only a single species, Palaeochenoides mioceanus, is known to date.

facts.statement: The first fossil assigned to Palaeochenoides mioceanus was a distal right femur found near the source of the Stono River in Charleston County, South Carolina.
facts.quote: The first fossil assigned to it – a distal right femur piece – was found near the source of the Stono River in Charleston County, South Carolina (United States).

facts.statement: The species name 'mioceanus' was originally a spelling error for 'miocaenus' meaning 'from the Miocene', reflecting an initial belief that the fossil came from the Early Miocene Hawthorne Formation.
facts.quote: At first it was believed to be from the Early Miocene Hawthorne Formation – its specific name, seemingly referring to the "Miocene ocean" as presumed habitat but actually a simple spelling error for "miocaenus", "from the Miocene", that was never corrected and hence became valid – alludes to this.

facts.statement: The genus name Palaeochenoides means 'ancient goose-like bird'.
facts.quote: The genus name, which means "ancient goose-like [bird]".

facts.statement: Comparisons of the femur showed Palaeochenoides resembled Anseriformes in one trait and 'higher waterbirds' like Pelecanidae in four out of five traits.
facts.quote: It was compared to that of Anserinae and Dendrocygninae (other Anseriformes were either similar to these or too unlike P. mioceanus), as well as with Pelecanidae, Phaethontidae and Phalacrocoraciformes of the "higher waterbird" radiation, and found to resemble the former in one, the latter in 4 out of 5 traits.

facts.statement: Early analysis proposed the bird was a large steganopod somewhat larger than the pelican species Pelecanus erythrorhynchos or P. onocrotalus.
facts.quote: The study proposed the fossil bird to have been "a large steganopod [...] somewhat larger than Pelecanus erythrorhynchos or P. onocrotalus,"

facts.statement: The fossil's thin-walled bone features a second toe trochlea attached kneewards and angled outwards, with a vestigial or missing hallux, typical of pseudotooth birds.
facts.quote: The thin-walled bone has a second toe trochlea that attaches notably kneewards from the others and is angled slightly outwards while the hallux was vestigial or missing, as is typical for the pseudotooth birds.

facts.statement: The bird presumably had a long, massive bill like its relatives, and its total length exceeded that of the largest pelicans.
facts.quote: Its bill was presumably long and massive as in its relatives, and in length the bird exceeded the largest pelicans.

facts.statement: As a presumed pelican relative, Palaeochenoides mioceanus was allied with Cyphornis and placed in the family Cyphornithidae.
facts.quote: Meanwhile, as a presumed pelican relative, P. mioceanus was allied with Cyphornis (another pseudotooth bird, known only from a proximal left tarsometatarsus) and placed in a family Cyphornithidae.

facts.statement: The family Cyphornithidae was subsequently assigned to the suborder Cladornithes.
facts.quote: This was subsequently assigned to a "pelecaniform" suborder Cladornithes.

facts.statement: Even if Cyphornis were the senior synonym of Palaeochenoides, the family name Pelagornithidae would remain unaffected by nomenclature rules.
facts.quote: And even if Cyphornis is the senior synonym of Palaeochenoides and Tympanoneisiotes (which is not overly likely due to size differences), according to the rules of zoological nomenclature the family name Pelagornithidae would not be affected.

facts.statement: The Paleobi Database lists Cyphornithidae as the parent group for Palaeochenoides.
The Paleobi Database classifies Palaeochenoides within the family Cyphornithidae.
The time range for Palaeochenoides is recorded as Serravallian to Serravallian, from 13.82 to 11.63 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Serravallian to Serravallian (13.82 to 11.63 million years ago)
